slides.title: Course Purpose: Get Rid of the Magic!
points: How do we encode information for them to “process” it?
What do they do while “processing” it?
How do they interact with memory while processing it?
What have been the major advancements in processor design?

slides.title: Abstract Course Learning Goals
points: You can explain to anyone (kids, experts, the uninterested) how an algorithm in a high-level language becomes executable instructions, and how a processor executes them
You can use the tools to compile and disassemble programs, and analyze assembly code
You know memory, processors and their architecture, and the main steps towards modern processors
You understand deeply that programs are simply instruction sequences that can be executed automatically
You can place the ways of programming computers, from machine code to AI coding assistants, in their historical context

aside.alt: A magnifying glass

slides.title: Detailed Course Learning Goals
slides.lead: Weeks 1 to 6: information representation and processing. Weeks 7 to 12: processors and memory.
rows: how different types of data are represented in binary
how electric circuits process binary data
how high-level program code becomes assembly instructions
reverse-engineer a compiled program and purposefully change its behavior
how a realistic instruction set architecture executes assembly instructions
simulate the execution of an assembly program on a given instruction set
how memory is organized, including the memory hierarchy and caching
reason about the memory architecture from the data of a memory-intensive program
the main advancements that led to modern processors, and their limits

slides.title: Information Representation in Computers

callout.text: What happens when π is represented (e.g., stored) in a computer system?

paragraphs: As you know, the accurate representation of the number π (3.1415…) is infinitely long.
Numbers that do not have infinite representations are affected as well!
Machine representations of numbers are finite approximations, and they can behave in unexpected ways.

aside.alt: Two formulas: unsigned addition UAdd is u plus v modulo 2 to the w; 2's complement addition TAdd adds or subtracts 2 to the w on negative or positive overflow

slides.title: Unsigned Addition and Negation

slides.title: Multiplication and Shifting
points: Multiplication (signed and unsigned): standard, ignoring the overflow bits
(x << k) multiplies by 2^{k}, both for signed and unsigned!

points.text: (x >> k) divides by 2^{k} and rounds down
sub: Unsigned: «logical shift» (shift in 0s)
Signed: «arithmetic shift» (shift in copies of the most significant bit)
Careful: for x < 0, this rounds towards minus infinity, but C integer division truncates towards zero

points: The compiler replaces multiplications and divisions by powers of two with (much faster) shift-and-add operations; for signed division, it first adds a bias

slides.title: Any Questions / Comments / Doubts / Concerns?
slides.heading: Take-Homes
points: Computers represent all information as finite sequences of bits, interpreted in context
Number representations (and all other data types) are necessarily finite
Programming languages use a fixed number of bits per instance (e.g., 32 bits for a C int)
Standards give the context: IEEE 754 (floating point), ISO 10646 «Unicode» (text), ISO 10918-1 (JPEG)
You can create your own mapping (but is it useful?)
